```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 110
)
library(heatwaveR)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Background

The functions `ts2clm()`, `detect_event()` and their `data.table`-only
counterparts `ts2clm3()`, `detect_event3()` treat each grid cell as an
independent time series. Run across a region, they produce a four-dimensional
boolean dataset of per-pixel events.

`detect_blob3()` reads that per-pixel result and identifies contiguous
heatwave-affected regions as 3-D connected components in (lon, lat, time),
under 6-connectivity (face-adjacent). For each component it returns:

- a per-event row with duration, voxel count, peak area, cumulative
  intensity-weighted volume (`cumI_km2_day`), and bounding box,
- a per-day row with area, area-weighted centroid, mean and max anomaly,
- optionally, the full footprint as one row per (event, lon, lat, date).

Events are ranked by a user-chosen metric (default `cumI_km2_day`, by
magnitude so the same default behaves correctly for cold spells).

## Input contract

`detect_blob3()` reads a long `data.table` from `detect_event3()` that has been
bound across grid cells. Each row is one (lon, lat, date) sample with the
columns `lon`, `lat`, `t`, `temp`, `seas`, `event`. The function does not run
the per-pixel detection itself; the user controls per-pixel arguments
(climatology window, `pctile`, `minDuration`) and any parallelisation outside.

## A worked example with synthetic data

Build a small 21 x 21 grid over 30 days and plant one spatially compact warm
patch and one isolated singleton:

```{r build-synth}
set.seed(2026)
lons  <- seq(0.0, 1.0, by = 0.05)
lats  <- seq(-32.0, -31.0, by = 0.05)
dates <- as.Date("2020-01-01") + 0:29
nx <- length(lons); ny <- length(lats); nt <- length(dates)

delta <- array(rnorm(nx * ny * nt, 0, 0.3), dim = c(nx, ny, nt))
delta[6:14, 6:14, 10:20] <- 3.0       # planted warm blob
delta[19, 18, 15]         <- 4.0       # high-intensity singleton

# Long form. Column-major order: i (lon) fastest, j (lat) middle, k (time) slowest.
long <- data.table(
  lon   = rep(lons, times = ny * nt),
  lat   = rep(rep(lats, each = nx), times = nt),
  t     = rep(dates, each = nx * ny),
  temp  = as.vector(delta),
  seas  = 0,
  event = as.vector(delta) > 1.5
)
sum(long$event)
```

Run the spatial detector:

```{r run}
res <- detect_blob3(long, topN = 5L, return = c("event", "daily", "voxel"))
res$event[, .(rank, blob, duration, n_voxels,
              peakArea_km2 = round(peakArea_km2, 1),
              cumI_km2_day = round(cumI_km2_day, 1),
              mean_delta = round(mean_delta, 2),
              max_delta  = round(max_delta, 2))]
```

The planted block ranks first. The singleton ranks second on intensity, even
though its volume is one voxel.

## Mapping the footprints

The daily area trajectory tells you how each event grew and shrank:

```{r daily-area}
top <- res$event[rank <= 3]
daily <- merge(res$daily, top[, .(blob, rank)], by = "blob")
ggplot(daily, aes(date, area_km2, colour = factor(rank))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "rank", option = "turbo") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression(Area ~ (km^2))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

The peak-day footprint as a raster, with a coastline if `sf` and
`rnaturalearth` are installed:

```{r footprint, fig.height = 4.5}
have_geo <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE) &&
            requireNamespace("rnaturalearth", quietly = TRUE)

top1   <- res$event[rank == 1]
vox1   <- res$voxel[blob == top1$blob & date == top1$date_peak]

p <- ggplot()
if (have_geo) {
  land <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = 50, returnclass = "sf")
  land_clip <- suppressWarnings(
    sf::st_crop(land, c(xmin = min(lons), xmax = max(lons),
                        ymin = min(lats), ymax = max(lats)))
  )
  p <- p + ggplot2::geom_sf(data = land_clip, fill = "grey92",
                            colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.2)
}
p +
  geom_raster(data = vox1, aes(lon, lat, fill = delta)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = expression(Delta), option = "inferno") +
  { if (have_geo) ggplot2::coord_sf(xlim = range(lons), ylim = range(lats), expand = FALSE)
    else coord_quickmap(xlim = range(lons), ylim = range(lats)) } +
  labs(title = sprintf("Top blob peak-day footprint: %s", top1$date_peak),
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

## Exporting an event as `sf` polygons

`blob_footprint()` converts the voxel table to an `sf` object, one polygon per
voxel by default, or one union per blob with `by = "event"`. This is the only
function in `heatwaveR` that touches `sf`.

```{r footprint-sf, eval = requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)}
foot <- blob_footprint(res$voxel, which = top1$blob, by = "event")
foot
```

The resulting `sf` object can be saved with `sf::st_write()` to GeoJSON, a
shapefile, or a GeoPackage for downstream GIS analysis.

## Cold spells

The function operates on a boolean event flag without inspecting polarity.
Pass per-pixel cold-spell input (from `detect_event3()` with `pctile = 10`)
to get cold-spell blobs. Signed metrics retain sign, and ranking by
`cumI_km2_day` uses magnitude so the most extreme cold spells appear first.

```{r mcs}
long_mcs <- copy(long)
long_mcs[, temp := -temp]              # flip to a synthetic cold-spell case
long_mcs[, event := temp - seas < -1.5]

res_mcs <- detect_blob3(long_mcs, topN = 3L)
res_mcs$event[, .(rank, blob, cumI_km2_day = round(cumI_km2_day, 1),
                  mean_delta = round(mean_delta, 2))]
attr(res_mcs$event, "polarity")
```

## Scaling to real gridded SST

In practice the input to `detect_blob3()` comes from a per-pixel application
of `detect_event3()` over a regional subset of OISST, OSTIA, or another daily
gridded SST product. The companion vignette `gridded_event_detection` shows
how to assemble that input from a NetCDF source. The per-pixel step is the
expensive one and is best parallelised over chunks of pixels; the spatial
detection runs in a single shot on the bound result.

## Memory and chunking

`detect_blob3()` allocates a 3-D integer mask of size `nx * ny * nt` plus a
matching label array. For a 0.05 degree grid over 2 years (the OSTIA East
Coast example), that is around 60 MB and 240 MB respectively, comfortable on
a laptop. For a 0.25 degree global grid over 30 years the allocations exceed
typical RAM. A chunked-along-time labelling routine with union-find stitching
across chunk boundaries is planned for a follow-up release.
